Authorization Mental Model & Threats
Separate identity from access and understand broken-access-control failure modes

Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Authenticated subject

v

Action

v

Resource

v

Context

v

Decision

Phase 19 transforms verified identity into contextual, server-side authorization decisions.

Authentication and authorization solve different problems
A valid bearer token proves the caller identity. It does not grant access to every row. Authorization evaluates the
subject, action, resource, and context. OWASP recommends least privilege, deny-by-default, and validating access on
every request.

Question                                         Layer

Who is calling?                                  SupabaseAuthGuard

Which TaskFlow user is that subject linked to?   AuthorizationService

Which workspace membership exists?               Membership relation

What may this role generally do?                 Role -> permission mapping

May this user act on this specific task?         Object-level policy / service logic

Broken access control is usually contextual

A user may be allowed to read Task objects in one workspace and forbidden from reading an identical Task object in another.
Type-level access alone is not enough.

Four useful models
• RBAC - role grants broad capabilities.

• Permission/claims model - actions such as task.delete or member.manage.

• ABAC - decisions include attributes such as project state or time.

• ReBAC/ownership - decisions depend on relationships: member-of, assigned-to, manager-of.

Create a safe bridge between external identity and application-domain authorization data

Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions

claims.sub

User.authSubject

v

User.id

Membership

Phase 19 transforms verified identity into contextual, server-side authorization decisions.

Link external identity to the application domain
Supabase Auth owns authentication identity. TaskFlow owns User, Membership, Workspace, Project, and Task. We
therefore add an explicit authSubject link instead of trusting email or stuffing all domain authorization into JWT claims.

model User {
id          String @id @default(uuid())
authSubject String? @unique
email       String @unique
// ...
}

Figure 1 - Identity mapping

Verified Supabase claims.sub

v

User.authSubject

v

TaskFlow User.id

v

Membership.userId

v

Workspace role + relationships

The external subject remains identity; the domain user remains application data.

Why nullable first?

Existing development rows already exist. Add the link as nullable, backfill trusted mappings, verify them, then consider making it
required in a later migration.

Do not link by ordinary request body
A browser must not be allowed to submit authSubject=user-X to claim another account. Linking is an onboarding/admin
concern performed through a trusted path.

lessons.body:
RBAC, Roles & Permission Matrix
Map workspace roles to explicit operations without scattering role checks

Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Membership role

v

Permission set

v

Coarse capability

Phase 19 transforms verified identity into contextual, server-side authorization decisions.

Role is a compact label; permission is the operation
TaskFlow already has workspace MembershipRole values OWNER, ADMIN, and MEMBER. Phase 19 maps those
roles to explicit permission names so controllers and services reason about actions rather than scattered if(role===...).

Operation                                                  OWNER                   ADMIN                   MEMBER

Read workspace/projects/tasks                              Yes                     Yes                     Yes

Create task                                                Yes                     Yes                     Yes

Update any task                                            Yes                     Yes                     No

Update assigned task                                       Yes                     Yes                     Yes

Delete task                                                Yes                     Yes                     No

Manage members                                             Yes                     Yes                     No

Manage workspace settings                                  Yes                     No                      No

export enum Permission {
TASK_READ = 'task.read',
TASK_CREATE = 'task.create',
TASK_UPDATE_ANY = 'task.update.any',
TASK_UPDATE_ASSIGNED = 'task.update.assigned',
TASK_DELETE = 'task.delete',
}

Do not put every permission in the JWT

Workspace roles can differ per workspace and change while a token is still valid. TaskFlow loads current application
authorization data from PostgreSQL instead of treating stale token claims as the whole policy.

NestJS Permission Metadata & Guards
Use Reflector metadata and guards for coarse workspace authorization

Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Auth guard

v

Permission metadata

v

Workspace membership

v

Controller

Phase 19 transforms verified identity into contextual, server-side authorization decisions.

NestJS metadata is useful for coarse route policy
NestJS officially supports RBAC and claims-style authorization with custom decorators, Reflector metadata, and
Guards. TaskFlow uses that pattern where a route has an explicit workspaceId and the required permission is known
before business execution.

export const RequireWorkspacePermissions =
Reflector.createDecorator<Permission[]>()

@Post()
@RequireWorkspacePermissions([Permission.PROJECT_CREATE])
createProject(...) { ... }

Default deny when the guard is applied
Our WorkspacePermissionsGuard refuses to proceed if it was explicitly attached but no permission metadata exists.
That catches a missing policy instead of silently allowing the route.

Figure 1 - Coarse permission guard

SupabaseAuthGuard verifies caller

v

WorkspacePermissionsGuard reads route metadata

v

workspaceId read from route params

v

Membership loaded from database

v

Role mapped to required permission

v

Controller runs

This works well when the authorization context is available before loading the resource.

Guards are not the whole authorization system

A task/:id route cannot safely authorize from a workspaceId supplied by the browser if the real Task belongs elsewhere.
Resource-level policy belongs after loading trusted resource context.

Object-Level Authorization & IDOR Defense
Scope actual database lookups by authenticated relationships

Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

User

v

Requested ID

v

Scoped Prisma query

v

Visible object only

Phase 19 transforms verified identity into contextual, server-side authorization decisions.

Object-level authorization prevents IDOR/BOLA
Changing /tasks/A to /tasks/B must never grant access simply because B is a syntactically valid ID. The server must
scope the actual database lookup by the authenticated user relationship.

const task = await prisma.task.findFirst({
where: {
id: taskId,
project: {
workspace: {
memberships: { some: { userId: user.id } },
},
},
},
})

Figure 1 - Secure lookup

Authenticated subject

v

Linked TaskFlow user

v

Requested task ID

v

Database query includes membership relation

v

Matching task returned OR no visible task

v

Authorization decision continues

The query itself helps enforce tenant/resource scope.

Why this is stronger than checking after findUnique
A global findUnique first reveals that the object exists and creates more room for accidental authorization omissions.
Scoped lookup makes the accessible dataset smaller by construction.

Ownership, Assignment & Service-Level
Policies
Enforce relationship-aware policies where trusted resource context exists

Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Resource context

v

Role permission

v

Assignment relationship

v

Allow/deny

Phase 19 transforms verified identity into contextual, server-side authorization decisions.

Ownership is a relationship, not a boolean
TaskFlow does not currently have a Task.ownerId. It has workspace membership and task assignment. We therefore
teach the real domain relationship instead of inventing an owner field just to demonstrate authorization.

Caller                              Task relationship                                      Update?

OWNER/ADMIN                         Workspace membership with update-any permission        Yes

MEMBER                              Task.assigneeId == current TaskFlow user               Yes

MEMBER                              Task assigned to another user or unassigned            No

if (ROLE_PERMISSIONS[role].has(Permission.TASK_UPDATE_ANY)) {
return true
}
return ROLE_PERMISSIONS[role].has(Permission.TASK_UPDATE_ASSIGNED)
&& task.assigneeId === user.id

Assignment is not authentication

assigneeId comes from database state after access-scoped loading. The browser cannot make itself the assignee by sending a
userId field and thereby bypass authorization.

Authorization and business rules compose
First decide whether the caller may attempt the operation. Then Phase 14 invariants still decide whether the operation
itself is valid. Permission does not bypass business rules.

401, 403, 404 & Error Contract
Use status semantics without leaking inaccessible resource existence

Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Authentication failure

v

Permission failure

v

Scoped not found

Phase 19 transforms verified identity into contextual, server-side authorization decisions.

401, 403, and 404 tell different security stories
TaskFlow keeps authentication failures, permission failures, and existence-hiding behavior distinct.

Situation                                                       Status           Reason

No/invalid access token                                         401              Identity not established

Authenticated workspace member lacks delete permission          403              Identity known; action forbidden

Task not visible in caller workspace scope                      404              Do not reveal whether an inaccessible task exists

404 is a policy choice, not a universal rule

For object lookups across tenant boundaries, hiding existence can reduce information disclosure. For an authenticated member
who can see the task but lacks a specific action, 403 is clearer.

Keep the Phase 13 error envelope
{
"statusCode": 403,
"code": "TASK_UPDATE_FORBIDDEN",
"message": "You may not update this task.",
"requestId": "...",
"path": "/tasks/..."
}

Membership Management & Privilege
Escalation
Protect the role and membership data that defines authorization itself

Phase 19 - Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Caller membership

v

Target membership

v

Role-change policy

v

Phase 19 transforms verified identity into contextual, server-side authorization decisions.

Membership management is itself privileged
If an ADMIN can assign OWNER arbitrarily, or a MEMBER can change their own role, the authorization system can be
bypassed through privilege escalation. Authorization rules must protect the policy data itself.

Action                                           Suggested TaskFlow policy

Invite/add MEMBER                                OWNER or ADMIN

Promote MEMBER -> ADMIN                          OWNER only (course policy)

Transfer OWNER                                   OWNER only with explicit workflow

Member changes own role                          Never directly

Remove OWNER while last owner                    Reject

Protect invariants around role changes
• Do not accept role from an untrusted ordinary update DTO without an authorization-specific endpoint.

• Load the caller membership and target membership from the same workspace.

• Prevent cross-workspace target IDs.

• Protect against removing the last OWNER.

• Audit high-impact role changes later in the production-hardening phases.

Least privilege applies to administration too

Admin is not automatically the same as owner. Separating sensitive workspace ownership actions reduces privilege escalation
blast radius.

Phase 19 transforms verified identity into contextual, server-side authorization decisions.

The same authorization model transfers to enterprise systems
Roles and resource relationships change by domain, but the reasoning pattern stays stable: subject + action +
resource + context.

Domain                     Authorization examples

HRIS                       Employee sees own payslips; HR sees employees in authorized scope; manager approves direct reports

RBAC alone eventually becomes insufficient
Real systems often combine role, ownership/relationships, attributes, monetary thresholds, workflow states,
department scope, and segregation-of-duties rules. Phase 19 teaches a simple architecture that can grow without
immediately adding a policy engine.

Scenario                                                                Expected

User 2 reads Workspace A task                                           200

User 2 updates task assigned to User 2                                  success

User 2 updates task assigned to User 1                                  403

User 2 deletes Workspace A task as MEMBER                               403

User 1 reads Workspace B task with no membership                        404/scoped not found

Design authorization for an HRIS leave request: employee can view own leave; supervisor can approve direct reports
only; HR can view department-wide; payroll can read approved leave dates but cannot approve; system must hide

• You can distinguish 401, 403, and scoped 404.

• You can map verified auth subject to a domain user safely.

Debugging Workshop — Phase 19: Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 19 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Enforce resource ownership, workspace membership, roles, and permissions on the API with server-side policies.

Required artifact
Permission model + guards/policies protecting TaskFlow workspace/task actions with deliberate 401/403/404 semantics.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can model permission checks by action/resource.
• Can test authorization matrixes.
• Can prevent IDOR.
• Can explain 401/403/404 choices.

Independent build sequence
1. List TaskFlow actions such as workspace.read, task.create, task.update, member.manage.
2. Map roles to capabilities without scattering role-name if statements across controllers.
3. Load membership for the relevant workspace and treat it as authorization evidence.
4. Enforce owner/member/role checks in server-side policy code.
5. Decide when 403 reveals too much and when a 404-style response better protects resource existence.
6. Write a matrix test covering at least owner, member, outsider, unauthenticated caller, and missing resource.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 19: Authorization, Ownership, RBAC & Permissions. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact

Acceptance criteria

- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

# TaskFlow Phase 19 Authorization Matrix

| Operation | OWNER | ADMIN | MEMBER |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Read workspace/projects/tasks | yes | yes | yes |
| Create task | yes | yes | yes |
| Update any task | yes | yes | no |
| Update assigned task | yes | yes | yes |
| Delete task | yes | yes | no |
| Create/update project | yes | yes | no |
| Manage members | yes | yes | no |
| Manage workspace settings | yes | no | no |

Notes:
- This is the course policy, not a universal RBAC model.
- Object-level checks still apply after role-to-permission mapping.
- A MEMBER being able to update assigned tasks is relationship-based, not just role-based.
- The server rechecks authorization on every request.

# Linking Supabase Auth identity to TaskFlow User

Phase 18 gives NestJS a verified Supabase subject (`request.user.id`).
Phase 19 must map that external identity to the domain `User` row used by Membership and Task relations.

Recommended migration:
1. Add `authSubject String? @unique` to `User`.
2. Run a migration.
3. Sign in with the development Supabase account and inspect `/auth/me` to obtain the verified `sub`.
4. Link that `sub` to the intended TaskFlow User row using a trusted admin/dev path (Prisma Studio, SQL, or a one-time script).
5. Do not accept `authSubject` from an ordinary browser request body.
6. After all real users are linked, consider making the column required in a later migration.
